The Indian squid Uroteuthis duvauceli begins life when the fertilised ovum develops into a paralarva that emerges from an egg capsule measuring up to 2.5 millimeters in diameter. Upon hatching, the neonatal individual possesses a minute mantle length of just 0.3 centimeters [Lb = 0.3 centimeters], a value derived from the maximum observed egg diameter. This minuscule size at birth places the hatchling among the smallest of the commercially exploited loliginids found in Indian coastal waters, reflecting the energetic constraints of yolk-dependent embryonic development. The initial post-hatching phase is characterised by rapid somatic growth as the young squid shifts to exogenous feeding on small crustaceans, a trophic switch that fuels a dramatic increase in body dimensions over the ensuing weeks.

Otolith microstructure analysis and laboratory rearing experiments have provided valuable insights into the species maximum recorded longevity. When maintained at a stable water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], female Uroteuthis duvauceli attain a terminal mantle length of 23 centimeters [Li = 23 centimeters] at the time of natural death, a body size that corresponds to an assumed lifespan of approximately two years. Males of the species, under identical thermal conditions, achieve a considerably larger final mantle length of 40 centimeters [Li = 40 centimeters] prior to senescence and mortality, also at two years of age. This pronounced sexual dimorphism in maximum size, with males nearly doubling the mantle length of females, is a common feature in loliginid squids and is likely linked to distinct reproductive strategies and agonistic behaviours among males competing for mating opportunities.

The onset of reproductive capability in Uroteuthis duvauceli is marked by the attainment of a specific body size threshold rather than a fixed chronological age. Field surveys and histological examination of gonadal tissue indicate that individuals reach puberty at a mantle length of 10 centimeters [Lp = 10 centimeters], at which point active gametogenesis begins. This size-based maturation schedule ensures that only individuals with sufficient somatic reserves direct resources toward reproductive effort. The transition from a juvenile, non-reproductive state to a sexually mature adult involves pronounced changes in organ systems, including the development of the hectocotylus in males and the enlargement of the nidamental glands in females. Puberty at this mantle length allows the population to maintain a high reproductive turnover, with individuals potentially spawning multiple times over their abbreviated adult phase.

Cumulative lifetime reproductive output has been estimated from captive spawning experiments conducted at a constant ambient temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. Under these controlled conditions, a single female Uroteuthis duvauceli deposits a total of 375,600 eggs  over the course of her reproductive life until natural death at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This extraordinarily high fecundity, characteristic of many pelagic squid species, reflects an r-selected life-history strategy wherein massive egg production compensates for high rates of early-life mortality in the planktonic environment. Each egg mass is spawned as a gelatinous finger-like capsule that is attached to the substrate, with individual capsules containing multiple ova arranged in a single layer. The total egg count underscores the substantial energetic investment required of females, who must forage intensively to sustain such elevated gamete production.

Female lifespan has been directly quantified in laboratory culture studies maintained at a stable thermal regime of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], revealing a maximum longevity of approximately 1095 days [am = approximately 1095 days]. This duration, equivalent to roughly three years, represents the period from hatching until senescence and organismal death, after which reproductive activity ceases entirely. The lifespan estimate is consistent with mortality schedules inferred from wild population length-frequency distributions, which suggest that few individuals survive beyond their second or third year. At this temperature, the species completes its entire life cycle rapidly, a trait that facilitates high population turnover and recruitment potential in the seasonally productive waters of the northern Indian Ocean. Environmental fluctuations, particularly in sea surface temperature, are likely to modulate this longevity, with cooler conditions potentially extending the lifespan at the cost of reduced growth rates.
